title: Is peer review doing its job?

turns.speaker: Rina
turns.text: Fourteen months from submission to acceptance. Two reviewers, one of whom clearly read the abstract and stopped.

turns.speaker: Paulo
turns.text: And it's unpaid, which is the fact that surprises people outside it.

turns.speaker: Anders
turns.text: Unpaid, done at midnight, by someone with their own deadlines. The wonder is that it works at all.

turns.speaker: Rina
turns.text: Does it, though? It very rarely catches fraud, because a reviewer sees a manuscript, not the underlying data.

turns.speaker: Anders
turns.text: It was never designed to catch fraud. It's meant to catch confusion and overreach, and it's reasonable at that.

turns.speaker: Anders
turns.text: The trouble is everyone outside treats publication as a stamp of truth rather than as a filter for obvious problems.

turns.speaker: Paulo
turns.text: Which journalists then report as fact, and the qualification never survives the headline.

turns.speaker: Rina
turns.text: Preprints are interesting here. Everything appears immediately and the reviewing happens in public afterwards.

turns.speaker: Paulo
turns.text: That worked well in some fields and badly during the pandemic, when the public was reading them.

turns.speaker: Anders
turns.text: The failure mode is different, not worse. Slow and hidden versus fast and messy.

turns.speaker: Rina
turns.text: Paying reviewers is the obvious fix nobody does.

turns.speaker: Paulo
turns.text: The publishers make enormous margins on work donated by the same academics who then buy it back.

turns.speaker: Anders
turns.text: Which is the part of the system that genuinely cannot be defended on any grounds.

points: Peer review is slow, with a fourteen-month example, and reviewing quality is uneven.
Reviewers are unpaid and work alongside their own commitments.
Rina notes it rarely catches fraud, since reviewers see manuscripts rather than data.
Anders argues it was designed to catch confusion and overreach, and the problem is outsiders treating publication as proof of truth.
Preprints reverse the order, publishing immediately with public review, which worked in some fields and poorly during the pandemic.
They agree publisher margins on donated academic labour, sold back to universities, are the least defensible part of the system.
